48863:
A genre is a kind of writing. We already know how genres work: we do not read a newspaper report, a love song and a cartoon in the same way. The Bible contains many genres. Narrative tells what happened, often without commenting on whether it was good (Judg 21:25). Law gives Israel's covenant instructions. Poetry, like the Psalms, speaks in images and emotion. Wisdom, like Proverbs, gives general truths for living. Prophecy calls God's people back to covenant faithfulness and speaks of what God will do. Gospels tell the life of Jesus as good news. Letters address particular churches and their problems. Apocalyptic, like Daniel and Revelation, uses dramatic symbols to unveil God's view of history.

Mistakes in genre lead to mistakes in meaning. A proverb read as a promise becomes a broken promise (Prov 22:6). A psalm of anger read as a command becomes a call to cruelty (Ps 137:9). A vision read as a newspaper becomes a timetable of news events. The deep study on hermeneutics walks through each genre in detail.
48864: Pictures and comparisons: figures of speech
48865:
A figure of speech says something in a non-literal way to make it more vivid or true to experience. The main ones in the Bible are these.

Analogy: explaining something by comparing it to something familiar ("as a father pitieth his children", Ps 103:13). Simile: an open comparison using "like" or "as" ("like a tree planted by the rivers", Ps 1:3). Metaphor: saying one thing is another ("The LORD is my shepherd", Ps 23:1; "Go ye, and tell that fox", Luke 13:32). Parable: a short story from everyday life that carries a surprise about God's kingdom (Luke 15:3-7). Imagery: a cluster of pictures that paint a scene, as in Psalm 18. Anthropomorphism: describing God with human features or feelings — his hand, eyes, smelling a sacrifice (Gen 8:21; Isa 59:1). The Bible itself warns that God "is not a man" (Num 23:19), so these are true pictures, not physical descriptions.

Hyperbole: deliberate exaggeration to make a point ("a camel to go through the eye of a needle", Mark 10:25). Merism: naming two opposites to mean everything between them ("the heaven and the earth" = all that exists, Gen 1:1; "my downsitting and mine uprising" = all I do, Ps 139:2). Idiom: a phrase whose meaning cannot be worked out from its words ("gird up the loins of your mind" = get ready for action, 1 Pet 1:13). Apocalyptic symbol: an image that stands for a reality, often explained in the text itself — the stars are angels and the lampstands are churches (Rev 1:20), the beasts are kings (Dan 7:17), and the Lion of Judah turns out to be a slain Lamb (Rev 5:5-6).
48866: The shape of the text: parallelism, chiasm and inclusio
48867:
Hebrew poetry does not rhyme sounds; it rhymes ideas. This is called parallelism: two or more lines that echo each other. In 1753 Robert Lowth described three types. Synonymous: the second line repeats the first in new words ("The heavens declare the glory of God; and the firmament sheweth his handywork", Ps 19:1). Antithetic: the second line gives the opposite ("A wise son maketh a glad father: but a foolish son is the heaviness of his mother", Prov 10:1). Synthetic: the second line develops or completes the first, as in the growing steps of walking, standing and sitting with the wicked (Ps 1:1). Later scholars such as James Kugel and Robert Alter show that the second line usually sharpens the first: "A — and what is more, B." So read the lines together, not as separate facts.

A chiasm is a pattern where ideas are given in one order and then repeated in reverse (A-B-B-A), often with the main point at the centre. "The sabbath was made for man, and not man for the sabbath" (Mark 2:27). In Hebrew, Genesis 9:6 runs "whoever sheds / the blood / of man // by man / his blood / shall be shed". Some scholars find chiasms across whole stories, such as the flood narrative, though they debate how many are intended.

An inclusio is a frame: a passage begins and ends with the same phrase to mark a unit and its theme. Psalm 8 opens and closes with "O LORD our Lord, how excellent is thy name in all the earth!" (Ps 8:1; Ps 8:9). The Beatitudes begin and end with "theirs is the kingdom of heaven" (Matt 5:3; Matt 5:10). Noticing the frame tells you what the whole passage is about.
48868: Irony and sarcasm: Jesus was not always gentle in tone
48869:
Irony says one thing while meaning another, often the opposite. Sarcasm is irony with a sharp edge. If we miss the tone, we can take a line to mean its opposite. The learner's notes rightly say that Jesus used sarcasm to expose religious views that hid God's heart.

"Ye blind guides, which strain at a gnat, and swallow a camel" (Matt 23:24) is hyperbole and sarcasm together: the religious leaders filter tiny insects from their drink but gulp down the largest unclean animal. "Full well ye reject the commandment of God, that ye may keep your own tradition" (Mark 7:9) uses the word *kalōs* ("well", "beautifully") ironically — most commentators hear it as "How skilfully you set aside God's command!" When warned that Herod wanted to kill him, Jesus said, "it cannot be that a prophet perish out of Jerusalem" (Luke 13:33): the holy city, of all places, is the one that kills its prophets (Luke 13:34).

The Bible's other voices do the same. Elijah mocks the prophets of Baal: perhaps your god is busy, or travelling, or asleep (1 Kgs 18:27). Paul tells the proud Corinthians, "Now ye are full, now ye are rich, ye have reigned as kings without us" (1 Cor 4:8). Sarcasm in Scripture is never cruelty for its own sake; it exposes pride and religious pretence so that people can see clearly.

48874: A strict literalist approach (rarely held consistently by anyone)
48875: God physically lowered the sky, stood on darkness and flew through the air seated on a winged creature during David's rescue. The problem: the historical accounts of David's escapes describe no such event (1 Sam 23:26-28), and the same reading would make God breathe smoke (Ps 18:8). Even most readers who call themselves literal treat these lines as poetry.

48878: This is storm-god imagery, the language neighbouring peoples used of Baal, the "rider of the clouds." Israel's poets claimed it for the LORD (Ps 68:4; Ps 104:3). The poem says: the true ruler of heaven and storm came down to save me. It is true poetry, not false science.
48880: Jewish and Christian commentators; the Talmudic principle that "the Torah speaks in the language of human beings" as applied by Maimonides
48881: The cherub is the bearer of God's throne, above the ark in the Holy of Holies (1 Sam 4:4) and in Ezekiel's vision (Ezek 10:1-22). The God enthroned in his temple left his throne in answer to one man's cry (Ps 18:6). The picture teaches God's majesty and his nearness at once.
48883: Church Fathers and Christ-centred readers today (e.g. Augustine on the Psalms; Brad Jersak, Brian Zahnd)

Yet he came not with smoke and arrows but in humility and self-giving love, showing what the storm imagery was always pointing toward: a God who comes down to rescue.

48972: Taking the Bible literally means taking it seriously
48973: Many believers feel that if they treat any passage as figurative, they are weakening the Bible. Taking every word literally feels like the safest and most faithful choice.
48974: The Bible's authors chose poems, parables, hyperbole and visions on purpose. Reading a psalm as a psalm is obeying the author, not doubting him. Jesus rebuked his disciples for being too literal when he spoke of the "leaven of the Pharisees" (Matt 16:6-12).

Their concern is that real history, such as the resurrection, not be turned into mere symbol (1 Cor 15:14). Both sides agree: read literally what is meant literally.
48976: Literalism can make the Bible look foolish to outsiders, can produce harm (Matt 5:29), and can hide the beauty and force of God's chosen ways of speaking.
48977: The "eye of the needle" was a small gate in Jerusalem
48978: A common sermon explanation says there was a small gate in Jerusalem's wall called "the Needle's Eye". A camel could squeeze through only by kneeling and removing its load, so the rich can enter the kingdom if they humble themselves.

Jesus used hyperbole to describe something impossible; the Babylonian Talmud uses a similar image of an elephant passing through a needle's eye (Berakhot 55b). The disciples understood him: "Who then can be saved?" Jesus answered, "With men it is impossible, but not with God" (Mark 10:26-27).

48997: The Bible was written for us but not to us. Every book was first spoken to real people in a real culture, time and language. 48998: Written for us, not to us
48999:
The Old Testament scholar John Walton often says that the Bible was written for us but not to us. The learner's notes say something similar: the Bible was not written to us but given to us. Every book had a first audience. Paul wrote to believers in Corinth, Rome and Philippi; the prophets spoke to Israel and Judah; Revelation was sent to seven named churches in Asia (Rev 1:4; Rev 1:11). We are reading someone else's letters, and the message reaches us through them.

This matters because writers leave out what their first readers already knew. When Paul writes "Now concerning the things whereof ye wrote unto me" (1 Cor 7:1), we are hearing one side of a conversation. When he speaks of "the present distress" (1 Cor 7:26), the Corinthians knew what he meant; we have to work it out. Walton's advice is that we must join the first audience in our imagination — learn what they knew — before we can hear how the text applies to us.

This is not a way of escaping the Bible's authority. It is a way of submitting to it. If God chose to speak through real people in a real time, then taking that time seriously is part of taking God seriously (Heb 1:1).
49000: Building the context: who, to whom, when, why
49001:
Context has several layers. The literary context is the paragraph, book and whole Bible around a verse. The historical context is the time, place and events. The cultural context is the shared customs and values. The language context is the words, idioms and grammar of Hebrew, Aramaic and Greek.

Dating can change the picture. Revelation is usually dated to about AD 95, near the end of the emperor Domitian's reign, following Irenaeus (*Against Heresies* 5.30.3); a minority of scholars date it to the late 60s under Nero. Either way it was written to churches facing pressure from Rome and its imperial cult, which shapes how we read its beasts and its call to endure (Rev 13:1-10; Rev 2:10). The book of Daniel is dated by traditional scholars to the 6th century BC and by most critical scholars to about 165 BC, during the persecution under Antiochus IV. Each dating leads readers to hear its visions differently (Dan 7:1-28). These are debated questions, and fair readers name them rather than hide them.

Purpose matters too. John tells us why he wrote: "that ye might believe that Jesus is the Christ" (John 20:31). Luke wrote so that Theophilus might know the certainty of what he had been taught (Luke 1:1-4). Knowing the purpose helps us see why a book includes some things and leaves out others.
49002: Cultural keys: honour, patronage, covenant and the ancient picture of the world
49003:
Honour and shame. In the ancient Mediterranean world, a person's worth was largely their public reputation in the eyes of family and village. Jesus "endured the cross, despising the shame" (Heb 12:2): crucifixion was meant to destroy honour, and the gospel turns that shame into glory. Many readers in South Asia, Africa and the Middle East feel this world immediately, because their own cultures are built around family honour.

Patronage and grace. Society ran on patrons (benefactors with resources) and clients (those who received favour and owed loyalty and praise in return). Jesus mentions rulers who are called "benefactors" (Luke 22:25), and a centurion is commended for building a synagogue (Luke 7:4-5). The Greek word for grace, *charis*, belonged to this world: a gift that creates a relationship and calls for a grateful response. Paul's "free gift" language (Rom 5:15) would have sounded like the generosity of the greatest patron of all.

Covenant. Israel's covenant with God echoes the treaty forms of the ancient Near East, where a great king recalls what he has done for a people and then sets out obligations, blessings and curses. Exodus 20 begins, "I am the LORD thy God, which have brought thee out of the land of Egypt" (Exod 20:2): rescue comes first, then commands. Deuteronomy's blessings and curses (Deut 28:1-68) follow the same pattern. Scholars debate whether Hittite or Assyrian treaties are the closer model.

Ancient cosmology. Ancient peoples pictured a solid dome (the "firmament", Hebrew *raqia*) holding back waters above (Gen 1:6-8), the earth set on pillars (1 Sam 2:8), with four corners (Isa 11:12; Rev 7:1). God spoke within that picture of the world to teach who made it and why, not to give a lesson in modern science. Readers disagree on how far this applies to Genesis 1, but most agree God did not first correct ancient cosmology before speaking.
49004: When an idiom loses its culture
49005:
An idiom is a phrase whose meaning comes from its culture, not from its individual words. Read without its culture, an idiom can mean something totally different — exactly the danger the learner's notes describe.

"If any man come to me, and hate not his father, and mother... he cannot be my disciple" (Luke 14:26). In Hebrew idiom, "love" and "hate" can mean "choose first" and "choose second". Jacob "loved also Rachel more than Leah", and Leah is then called "hated" (Gen 29:30-31). Matthew reports the saying as "He that loveth father or mother more than me" (Matt 10:37). "Jacob have I loved, but Esau have I hated" (Mal 1:2-3; Rom 9:13) is about choosing, not emotion. The "horn of my salvation" (Ps 18:2; Luke 1:69) means mighty strength, from the image of a strong animal's horns. When the KJV speaks of the "bowels of Jesus Christ" (Phil 1:8), it renders the Greek *splanchna*, the inner organs, which were seen as the seat of deep feeling; modern versions say "affection" or "compassion".

Some idioms are still debated. "Thou shalt heap coals of fire upon his head" (Prov 25:21-22; Rom 12:20) has been read as burning shame that leads to repentance, as a link to an Egyptian ritual in which a penitent carried coals on the head (known from a late Demotic text), or as simple generosity — giving live coals to a neighbour whose fire has gone out. All agree on the context: overcome evil with good (Rom 12:21).
